title: The Tribes’ Request • Treachery in the Pass • Khubayb’s Last Two Rak‘ahs

blocks.1: A few months passed after Uhud. Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa‘dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram. Madinah had some relief then. At that time two delegations from two tribes came to Madinah. One from the tribes of ‘Adal and al-Qarah, the other from the tribe of ‘Amir ibn Sa‘sa‘ah. Both groups said almost the same thing: Islam is spreading among us, send some of your Companions, they will teach us the religion and have us recite the Qur’an.{{1}}
blocks.2: The Prophet {{1}} accepted both requests. With the first group he sent ten Companions. With the second, seventy.{{2}}
blocks.3: Both groups had lied. An eagerness to learn the religion; few requests sound more beautiful. Precisely behind this cover lay the deepest conspiracy. The Prophet {{1}} believed, because treachery was not in his nature; he had never learned to search for a plot in anyone’s word. When we are deceived once, afterwards we look for suspicion in everyone’s words. Yet another’s deceit can never be a reason for changing our own honesty.
blocks.5: The leader of those who went with ‘Adal and al-Qarah was ‘Asim ibn Thabit (RA). With him were Khubayb ibn ‘Adi (RA), Zayd ibn al-Dathinnah (RA), ‘Abdullah ibn Tariq (RA) and a few others. Although they were called with talk of teaching the religion, this group entering unfamiliar territory is described in the hadith as a reconnaissance expedition; after Uhud, caution was only natural. As soon as they reached a watering place of Hudhayl named Raji‘, the group betrayed them; those they had called to teach the religion shouted and brought Hudhayl, to attack their own guests.{{1}}
blocks.7: The Messenger of Allah {{1}} sent ten men as a scouting party, and appointed as their commander ‘Asim ibn Thabit al-Ansari, the grandfather of ‘Asim ibn ‘Umar. They set out, and when they reached a place called al-Hada’ah between ‘Usfan and Makkah, news of them was given to a branch of Hudhayl called Banu Lihyan. About two hundred men, all archers, followed them, tracing their marks, even seeing the date stones they had left behind and saying, these are the dates of Madinah. In the end they caught up with them.{{2}}
blocks.8: ‘Asim (RA) and his companions took refuge on a high mound. The enemy surrounded them and said, come down, we promise you, we will not kill even one. ‘Asim (RA) said, I will not come down today under the protection of a disbeliever. O Allah, inform Your Prophet of our news. They shot arrows. ‘Asim (RA) was martyred with seven others. Left were Khubayb (RA), Zayd (RA), and a third, ‘Abdullah ibn Tariq (RA).{{1}}
blocks.9: ‘Asim’s (RA) prayer was accepted that very day. The news reached the Prophet {{1}} of what had happened to ‘Asim (RA) and his companions.{{2}}
blocks.10: At Badr, two sons of Sulafah bint Sa‘d, a woman of Makkah, had been killed by ‘Asim (RA). In revenge she had vowed to drink wine from ‘Asim’s (RA) skull.{{1}}
blocks.12: When some disbelievers of Quraysh heard that ‘Asim (RA) had been killed, they sent men to bring some part of his body, so he could be recognized; because on the day of Badr he had killed one of their great leaders. But Allah sent a swarm of insects, like a cloud, over ‘Asim (RA), which protected him from their messenger; they could not cut anything from his flesh.{{1}}
blocks.13: In his lifetime ‘Asim (RA) had vowed that no polytheist would touch him, and he would not touch any polytheist. When ‘Umar (RA) heard that the bees had protected his body, he would say, Allah protects His believing servant.{{1}}
blocks.14: ‘Asim (RA) kept one vow all his life. After his death Allah kept that same vow for him. The vow we forget, assuming no one will remember, that is exactly what Allah remembers.
blocks.16: Khubayb (RA), Zayd (RA) and the third softened, surrendered in hope of living, on the condition of a word and a promise. The word was not kept. They were bound with bowstrings and taken away. The third freed his hands and said, this is the first betrayal. He refused to go along. They pulled and tugged but could not persuade him; they stoned him and killed him right there.
blocks.18: They took Khubayb (RA) and Ibn al-Dathinnah away, and sold them in Makkah after the Battle of Badr. The sons of al-Harith ibn ‘Amir ibn Nawfal bought Khubayb (RA); on the day of Badr it was Khubayb (RA) who had killed al-Harith ibn ‘Amir. Khubayb (RA) remained a captive with them.{{1}}
blocks.19: Month after month he remained a captive. Al-Harith’s daughter herself later used to narrate those days.
blocks.21: When they gathered to kill him, he asked me to lend him a razor, to cleanse his body. I lent it to him. Meanwhile one of my sons, without my noticing, had gone to him. I saw the boy sitting on his lap, the razor in his hand. I was so startled that Khubayb (RA) understood it from my face. He said, are you afraid I will kill him? I would not do that. By Allah, I have never seen a better captive than Khubayb (RA). By Allah, one day I saw him eating from a bunch of grapes in his hand, though he was bound in iron, and there was no fruit anywhere in Makkah. It was surely provision from Allah, which He had given to Khubayb (RA).{{1}}
blocks.22: A captive who would be killed in a few days, in his hand a sharp razor and an innocent child. The mother, watching from a distance, gasped. Yet in the captive’s mind there was not the slightest evil thought toward the child. The person who even in the last moments of their life guards another’s trust needs no further proof of their character. There was no fruit anywhere in Makkah, yet in his hand a bunch of grapes. Even when all the doors of people close, Allah’s door does not close. Allah had not forgotten even the provision of a prisoner in chains. In the end he was taken away to be killed.
blocks.24: When they took him out of the Haram to kill him, Khubayb (RA) said to them, let me pray two rak‘ahs. They let him go, and he prayed two rak‘ahs. Then he said, by Allah, were it not that you would think I am prolonging this out of fear of death, I would have prolonged it more. O Allah, count them one by one. And I do not care, so long as I die a Muslim, on whichever side my body falls in the way of Allah. This is for Allah alone; if He wills, He will bless every severed limb of my torn body. Then Ibn al-Harith stood up and killed him. Standing before death, Khubayb (RA) was the first Muslim who established this practice of two rak‘ahs for every Muslim killed as a captive.{{1}}
blocks.25: Before being crucified Khubayb (RA) also said some words, in the rhythm of poetry.
blocks.27: To Allah I complain of my loneliness, then my distress, and of what the enemies have prepared for me at my death. The fear of death does not make me tremble, I will die anyway; my fear is only of the blazing fire of Hell.{{1}}
blocks.28: One who can speak of his loneliness even before death, it would be wrong to say there was no fear in his heart. There was fear, but the place of that fear was right. Not the death of the world, but the fire of the Hereafter. A deed begins from need, then becomes a custom. Two rak‘ahs before a martyr, still in this Ummah’s memory. Mu‘awiyah (RA), still a polytheist then, was in the crowd that day. Later he used to say, hearing Khubayb’s (RA) curse I lay down on the ground in fear.{{1}}
blocks.29: Another was Sa‘id ibn ‘Amir (RA), still a polytheist then. Many years later he was an amir appointed by ‘Umar (RA) in Syria. Once the people of Hims went to ‘Umar (RA) and made four complaints against their amir: that he comes out only after much of the day has passed, that he does not answer anyone’s call at night, that one day a month he does not show himself at all, and that now and then he faints. ‘Umar (RA) asked the reasons one by one. Sa‘id (RA) said, I have no servant; I knead the dough myself, bake the bread, then come out, so I am late. I have kept the day for the people, and the night I have kept only for the worship of Allah. And that one day a month, I have only one garment, I am delayed in coming out waiting for it to be washed and dried. Then the answer to the fourth complaint: in Makkah I saw Khubayb’s death scene with my own eyes. Quraysh was wounding his body with knives, yet asked, would you want Muhammad in your place? He said, by Allah, I would not want to sit among my family while even a thorn pricks Muhammad {{1}}. That day I did not help him; that memory is what sometimes makes me faint.{{2}}
blocks.30: Hearing all four answers ‘Umar (RA) was pleased and sent a thousand dinars in Sa‘id’s (RA) name. Sa‘id (RA) gave away all of it among widows, orphans and the needy, keeping with himself only one gold coin. An ordinary subject complaining to the caliph about his appointed amir, the caliph listening attentively to that complaint, summoning the amir to account; this very scene is a picture of ‘Umar’s (RA) rule. A scene can haunt a person all their life. That day Sa‘id (RA) was a polytheist; later he accepted Islam, and became ‘Umar’s (RA) beloved amir too. Yet the weight of that scene did not lift.

footnotes.1: The number of the first group: ten in Sahih al-Bukhari 3045 (sahih); six in the Sirah-based narration of Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir. The number of the second group: seventy in Sahih al-Bukhari 4090 (sahih); forty in Ibn Ishaq’s Sirah-based narration. The main text takes the number from the sahih source.
footnotes.2: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Raji‘’ (‘ghadaru bihim fa-istasrakhu ‘alayhim Hudhaylan’; it was the group of ‘Adal and al-Qarah who called Hudhayl to attack). Sirah-based.
footnotes.5: Sahih al-Bukhari 3045 (‘fa-stajaba Allah li-‘Asim ibn Thabit yawma usiba, fa-akhbara al-Nabi {{1}} ashabahu khabarahum wa ma usibu’).
footnotes.6: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Raji‘’ (the vow of Sulafah bint Sa‘d). Sirah-based.
footnotes.8: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Raji‘’ (‘Asim’s resolve and ‘Umar’s (RA) remark; the main event is in Sahih al-Bukhari 3045, the explanation of the resolve is Sirah-based).
footnotes.10: Sahih al-Bukhari 3045 (the narration of al-Harith ibn ‘Amir’s daughter, from ‘Ubaydullah ibn ‘Iyad)
footnotes.12: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Raji‘’ (two more lines of Khubayb’s (RA) poem: ‘ila Allah ashku ghurbati thumma kurbati’ and ‘wa ma bi hidhar al-mawt inni lamayyitun’; only the earlier two lines ‘falastu ubali hina uqtalu Muslimanan’ are in Sahih al-Bukhari 3045, this part is Sirah-based).
footnotes.13: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Raji‘’ (the statement of Mu‘awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan; the Arabs used to think that lying down on one side at the time of a curse avoids it). Sirah-based.
footnotes.14: Abu Nu‘aym, Hilyat al-Awliya’ (chain: Muhammad ibn ‘Abdillah ← al-Hasan ibn ‘Ali ibn Nasr al-Tusi ← Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Karim al-‘Abdi ← al-Haytham ibn ‘Adi ← Thawr ibn Yazid ← Khalid ibn Ma‘dan); also mentioned in al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah. **Caution:** here, in Sa‘id’s (RA) account, the saying ‘let not a thorn prick’ has come in Khubayb’s name, yet in an earlier part of this same dars (note 2012) almost the very same words have come in the name of Zayd ibn al-Dathinnah through Ibn Ishaq. Since both were asked the same question, both may have given answers of the same pattern, or the names may have been swapped in the narration; which is correct cannot be said with certainty, so both narrations have been kept independently.

quiz.q: After Uhud, which two tribes sent delegations to Madinah asking for Companions?
o: ‘Adal-al-Qarah and ‘Amir ibn Sa‘sa‘ah
Banu Lihyan and Banu Sulaym
Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah
Ri‘l, Dhakwan, ‘Usayyah and Banu Lihyan

quiz.q: Though the ‘Adal-al-Qarah tribe asked for Companions in the name of learning da‘wah, what was their real aim?
o: Really learning the religion and returning to their own tribe
Building a permanent alliance with Madinah
Handing them over to Quraysh to receive a reward
Asking for some weapons for use in war

quiz.q: From the incident of the Raji‘ expedition, what caution can be taken in today’s life?
o: Every offer of help should be rejected without consideration
To regard every stranger with suspicion
To trust only those of blood relation
Not to trust without verifying merely because someone’s offer sounds sweet
quiz.e: Sahih al-Bukhari 3045; Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir.

quiz.q: According to Sahih al-Bukhari, how many were in the party of ‘Asim ibn Thabit (RA)?
o: Six
Ten
Forty
Seventy

quiz.q: What did Allah send to protect ‘Asim’s body?
o: A fierce storm
A guarding band of angels
A swarm of insects like bees
Heavy rain for several days in a row

quiz.q: What lay behind ‘Asim (RA) refusing to surrender?
o: The prospect of victory still looking bright
A strict instruction received from companions before the fight began
A fierce desire to take revenge on the enemy
A resolve not to rely on the promise of any disbeliever

quiz.q: Though the polytheists wanted to mutilate ‘Asim’s body, why could they not?
o: A swarm of insects like bees stood guard around the body
In the deep darkness of night the body was moved away somewhere
The companions guarded the body all night
The polytheists became frightened and left the place

quiz.q: What lesson does ‘Asim’s (RA) saying ‘I will not come down under a disbeliever’s protection’ give in today’s life?
o: Never to compromise on self-respect and the principles of the religion
To avoid every kind of compromise in life
To refuse others’ help even in time of need
That it is always better to carry on the fight alone

quiz.q: Who bought Khubayb and Zayd in Makkah?
o: Abu Sufyan and his wife Hind bint ‘Utbah
Umayyah ibn Khalaf and his son
Some members of Abu Jahl’s family
The sons of al-Harith and Safwan ibn Umayyah
quiz.e: Sahih al-Bukhari 3045; Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir.

quiz.q: What did Khubayb ask for before death?
o: Permission to pray two rak‘ahs
Permission to send a letter to his family
Permission to drink water
Time to write poetry

quiz.q: According to the hadith, who established the practice of two rak‘ahs for a Muslim killed as a captive?
o: ‘Asim ibn Thabit (RA)
Khubayb ibn ‘Adi (RA)
Zayd ibn al-Dathinnah (RA)
‘Abdullah ibn Tariq (RA)

quiz.q: What was the main reason al-Harith’s family bought Khubayb?
o: To make him an ordinary slave and sell him again
The desire to take revenge for al-Harith, killed at Badr
To collect a large ransom in time
To extract news of Madinah from him

quiz.q: What does the scene of a bunch of grapes in Khubayb’s hand, at a time when there was no fruit in Makkah, indicate?
o: He had bought it from the market with his saved money
One of the guards had kindly given it as a gift
It was an inexplicable provision from Allah
He himself had planted a small grapevine

quiz.q: From the request to pray two rak‘ahs before death, what priority of Khubayb is understood?
o: To remember his family one last time
To waste the enemy’s time and look for an opportunity
To postpone the death sentence in hope of help
Placing prayer before everything even at the mouth of death

quiz.q: From Khubayb’s eagerness for prayer even in his last moments, what can we learn today?
o: Prayer can be postponed at times of danger to life
To put prayer first even in the hardest time
Prayer is a deed only for healthy, safe times
If there is fear of death, prayer may be abandoned

quiz.q: From Khubayb’s poetry and firmness, what can be learned in today’s hard times?
o: Expressing pain is itself a kind of weakness
To think that protest is always the only right path
One can express steadfastness in faith even amid hardship
It is best to stay completely silent in times of danger
